newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S, Britain ready to join Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: U.S, Britain ready to join Zaire force.

text.p: The United States and Britain said on Wednesday they were prepared to join a U.N. military operation to save lives in war-hit eastern Zaire, ending days of uncertainty over the mission.
In Kigali, Rwanda's president gave a warning that the intervention could go the way of other ill-fated missions to Africa unless Rwandan-backed Zairean rebels were consulted.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said the U.S. commitment, which was expected to last about four months, involves dispatching 1,000 ground troops to the African nation. Several thousand additional troops would be sent to the region to help with support activities, he said.

"The president has decided that the United States is willing, in principle, to participate in a limited fashion in this mission as long as certain conditions are stipulated to," McCurry said at a White House briefing.
Among the conditions he listed were that the mission would be of limited duration and made up of a multinational force.
In London, Britain said it was ready to contribute troops but Prime Minister John Major said vital details about the international mission still needed to be worked out.

"Ministers agreed the UK should be ready to contribute constructively to the international response, including to a multinational force, providing a satisfactory plan can be worked out," a statement from Major's office said on Wednesday.

The statement was released after a meeting of ministers at Major's official London home and ended a week of hesitation by Britain, once a major colonial power in Africa, about becoming involved in an area it believes is not its "back yard".

"We will contribute, we will definitely send troops," Major told reporters later. But he said how many troops Britain would send, what the scope of the mission would be and what its "exit strategy" would be were questions still to be answered.
Canada has offered to lead the multilateral military force to bring in aid to desperate Rwandan and Burundian Hutus, some cut off from help since local Tutsis rebelled a month ago.
The announcements in London and Washington clear the way for the U.N. Security Council to work on a resolution, drafted by Canada, in hopes it can be adopted by the end of the week.
France which led the intervention lobby but which is seen by Rwanda as partisan in the Hutu-Tutsi conflict behind much of the bloodletting in Central Africa, welcomed the U.S. decision.

It said it was prepared to send 600 paratroopers to Zaire within 24 hours of U.N. approval for a multinational force to help starving refugees and have 600 more there a day later, defence officials said on Wednesday.

"France welcomes this (U.S.) decision, which will enable the force to get off the ground without delay and dispatch humanitarian aid to those people who are in distress," the ministry said in a statement.

Rwandan President Pascal Bizimungu insisted in an interview with Reuters that Tutsi rebels who defeated the Zaire army in two provinces where camps for Hutu refugees were located, must be consulted, something Zaire opposes strongly.
"If they do not negotiate this with the rebels then they will be declaring war and it will be messy," the president, a member of the Hutu majority, added in an interview.
In an ominous development, Uganda reported it had repulsed an attack by Zairean soldiers and Zaire-based Ugandan dissidents on two border posts in the southwest of the country.

Zaire denied the allegation and repeated charges that Uganda, along with the Tutsi-led governments of Rwanda and Burundi, were backing the Banyamulenge Tutsis who started battling the Zaire army on October 18.
